messages.author: 89729ecad9822a0d
messages.subject: temporal scale of abundance estimates
parts:
Hello,


In a passive acoustic abundance estimation method evaluation study, I compared the results of several SECR analyses (among other statistical approaches) to a census of bottlenose dolphins. I have census data available at 3 different temporal scales (instantaneous, daily, and total abundance/abundance over the entire study period). For this study, it is imperative that the resulting SECR estimate is compared to census results on the correct temporal scale (they are all different). As such, would you mind verifying that this is the case for the following SECR analysis structures?


First, a quick background: In each case, data was collected within the same study area and period. 2-3 autonomous acoustic recorders were systematically moved every day (25 days) until all survey point locations (systematic survey design) were sampled. The sound of interest used for each analysis is the bottlenose dolphin signature whistle.


1.      In the first analysis, abundance was estimated in an animal-based context (animals can be individually identified using their signature whistles). Each day was considered a separate session (and therefore had a unique ID per session). Variation in deployment duration was incorporated by using a trap layout file for each session (or day). Am I correct in assuming that this gives me a daily abundance estimate?

Note: When this was attempted using day as an occasion, instead of session, and animals were instead given unique ID’s per session, the result was approximately 25 times the true daily abundance. It appears that this approach ‘reset’ the home range centers for each occasion, and produced an estimate that was the sum of daily abundance estimates on each day?


2.      In the second analysis, a non-Euclidean SECR was performed in a cue-based context, where no attempt was made to distinguish between animals (only cues). In this case, a day was considered an occasion. The cue rate modifier was scaled up from a per minute rate to a per day rate, for a comparable estimate. This was done using the average deployment duration over the study period. It has been argued that this approach produces an instantaneous abundance estimate. However, I believe that it gives me a daily abundance estimate. Is this a correct assumption? I know that it is typical for the recording period per occasion to be of a much shorter duration than one day. There is no way to distinguish, for example, between one animal vocalizing within range of the recorders all day, and 10 animals that are there for a much shorter period, if both scenarios result in the same total number of cues. This could therefore lead to me overestimating animal abundance, particularly if the former scenario is common. The results of this analysis were very similar to the true daily abundance. I think that this is the case because animals typically did not spend more than a few minutes at a time within acoustic range of deployed recorders. However, I would like to make sure that this was not mere coincidence. Can you help me by clarifying this?


Thanks!

Goldie

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: temporal scale of abundance estimates
parts:
Hello Goldie
Sorry for the delay here - I've been travelling and I rather hoped some of the other experts on the group might help.
Firstly, did you really just have 2-3 recorders in your array? That will be limiting.

I am uneasy with the concept 'daily abundance' - I prefer to think in terms of instantaneous density or average instantaneous density. The first analysis should deliver an estimate of the (average) population density, but there are various ways this could screw up. If the movements of dolphins over the duration of monitoring are on a scale larger than your array extent (which seems to be true) then SECR probably won't help. Also, in a combined (daily occasion) analysis you should use the usage attribute of the traps object to show how sites were monitored day by day. Splitting into daily 'sessions' is a possible solution (the scale of each daily array may better match the scale of daily movements), but I would tread carefully and possibly simulate some data.

Regarding the second (cue-based) analysis - cues are (virtually) instantaneous, and it seems pretty obvious that the longer you monitor the more you count, the larger the estimated cue density (cues per unit area), and the larger the adjustment (per capita cue rate times duration) that must be applied to infer population density. Maybe it will help to specify the units of the quantities you are working with.

Murray

messages.subject: Re: temporal scale of abundance estimates
parts:
Hi Murray,

 

No worries! I actually did get a helpful response from another group member.


To answer your question, yes, unfortunately, I was limited to only a few recorders.


Thanks for your suggestion of simulating data. I did incorporate effort into both the daily occasion and daily session analyses. However, I think that simulating data will prove useful.


Regarding the cue-based analysis, I totally agree that the longer you monitor, the larger the cue density, and the larger the adjustment required to convert to animal density. The part that I was confused about was whether the resulting density estimate would be an instantaneous one, or an average daily density estimate. I was under the impression that the resulting SECR cue density is the average density per occasion (or day, in my case), and not per instant in time. So, if I monitored for 1 hour, my cue density estimate would be per hour. However, based on what you are saying, the resulting estimate is instantaneous and independent of time (provided I use an appropriate cue rate modifier), correct? If so, and I did want to obtain the average number of animals that occupied the bay per occasion/day, and not per instant in time, which would be time dependent, how would I do this within the SECR framework?

 

Thanks!

Goldie

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: temporal scale of abundance estimates
parts:
Perhaps you could share the response from the other group member.
Density is measured in animals per unit area, whether instantaneous or averaged over time. So 'density per day' doesn't mean anything to me. Cue density is measured in cues per unit area per unit time (cues are ephemeral, animals aren't). Dividing cue density by per capita cue rate (cues per unit time) gives you an estimate of animal density; if based on cues accumulated over a period of time I suppose it is a sort of average, but it still has density units (animals per unit area).
Murray

messages.author: 436d107e7e3e44df
messages.subject: Re: temporal scale of abundance estimates
parts:
Hi, 

I initially responded to Goldie. Our discussion has boiled down to similar to the above: It comes down to how you define density. Acoustic SECR methods give a cue density (cues per unit time per unit space), and dividing by cue rate (cues per individual per unit time) gives an "average" animal density for an instantaneous moment in time. This approach will not be able to tell you whether you have one individual occupying a site 24 hours a day, or ten individuals each occupying the site for 2.4 hours per day, for example.

In order to answer questions like "how many animals visit this site per day?" you therefore need to know something about animal movement. In principle, if it is possible to identify animals from their calls, SECR could potentially estimate movement parameters from acoustic data -- the detection locations of a sequence of cues from the same individual would provide information about how the animal is moving through the acoustic array. However, (1) you would probably need a fairly dense array of recorders to get enough information to make this worthwhile, and (2) nobody has come up with a method to fit such a model yet.

Estimating movement parameters using an acoustic SECR model is similar to the movement of animal activity centres in non-acoustic SECR (e.g., Royle et al, Ergon and Gardner). However, as I see it, there is one fairly substantial complication: When using a robust-design approach you know when you failed to detect an individual (you set some traps out for a number of occasions within a session and didn't see it), but in an analogous acoustic SECR situation you don't (if you fail to detect an animal for an extended period of time, you don't know if it is because the animal has moved away from the detectors, or if it just hasn't produced a call). I think deriving the likelihood for such a situation would require integration over all possible movement paths an animal may have taken between detected calls, which is possibly computationally intractable (or, at the very least, extremely difficult).

If you're really interested in estimating how many individuals use the site per day (I guess maybe this is some sort of "density per day", but I'm not really sure what this would mean, either), then you're probably best off estimating the movement parameters from independent data (e.g., telemetry). But then of course you have all the issues being mentioned in the parallel discussion on this list -- you have to make sure you are getting a representative sample from your population, and so on.

Cheers,

Ben

On Mon, Sep 19, 2016 at 7:39 PM, Murray Efford <murray...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hello Goldie
Sorry for the delay here - I've been travelling and I rather hoped some of the other experts on the group might help.
Firstly, did you really just have 2-3 recorders in your array? That will be limiting.

I am uneasy with the concept 'daily abundance' - I prefer to think in terms of instantaneous density or average instantaneous density. The first analysis should deliver an estimate of the (average) population density, but there are various ways this could screw up. If the movements of dolphins over the duration of monitoring are on a scale larger than your array extent (which seems to be true) then SECR probably won't help. Also, in a combined (daily occasion) analysis you should use the usage attribute of the traps object to show how sites were monitored day by day. Splitting into daily 'sessions' is a possible solution (the scale of each daily array may better match the scale of daily movements), but I would tread carefully and possibly simulate some data.

Regarding the second (cue-based) analysis - cues are (virtually) instantaneous, and it seems pretty obvious that the longer you monitor the more you count, the larger the estimated cue density (cues per unit area), and the larger the adjustment (per capita cue rate times duration) that must be applied to infer population density. Maybe it will help to specify the units of the quantities you are working with.

Murray
